Maths at work

Health and science

Jobs in this route, and the maths they use.

Ratio

Hospital nurse

Health and science

\(\displaystyle \text{dose} = \dfrac{\text{want}}{\text{have}} \times \text{volume}\)

How many ml is a 125 mg dose?

Liquid medicine comes at a strength, such as 250 mg in 5 ml. Nurses use: volume = what you want ÷ what you have × what it is in. The prescription is 125 mg. The bottle says 250 mg in 5 ml.

  1. \(125 \div 250 = 0.5\).
  2. \(0.5 \times 5 = 2.5\) ml.

The answer: \(125 \div 250 \times 5 = 2.5\) ml

Percentages

Football performance analyst

Health and science

\(\displaystyle \dfrac{\text{completed}}{\text{attempted}} \times 100\)

Is this midfielder's passing any good?

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

Analysts turn a match into numbers the coach can use. A midfielder tried 480 passes over five games and 408 reached a teammate (example figures).

  1. Pass completion: \(408 \div 480 \times 100 = 85\%\).

The answer: \(408 \div 480 \times 100 = 85\%\)

Averages and statistics

Practice nurse

Health and science

\(\displaystyle \bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x}{n}\)

Why isn't one blood pressure reading enough?

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

One blood pressure reading can mislead, so NICE says to take readings at home, twice a day for 4 to 7 days, ignore the first day, and use the mean of the rest. After day 1, the top (systolic) numbers are 138, 134, 136, 140, 132, 136 (example figures).

  1. Add them: 816.
  2. Mean: \(816 \div 6 = 136\).
  3. The doctor compares that average, with the clinic reading, against NICE's limits.

The answer: \(816 \div 6 = 136\)

Health visitor

Health and science

What does "the 91st centile" mean for this baby?

Babies' weights are plotted on growth charts with centile lines. A centile shows how many healthy children are expected to be below that line. A baby is on the 91st centile.

  1. 91 out of 100 healthy babies the same age are expected to weigh less.
  2. \(100 - 91 = 9\) out of 100 are expected to weigh more.

The answer: \(100 - 91 = 9\) in 100 weigh more

Performance sports scientist

Health and science

\(\displaystyle \dfrac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \times 100\)

Has six weeks' training actually worked?

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

Sports scientists analyse training data to see if an athlete is improving. One jump can be a fluke, so they use the mean of several. Five jumps before training: 38, 41, 39, 42, 40 cm (example figures). After six weeks the mean is 42 cm.

  1. Total: \(38 + 41 + 39 + 42 + 40 = 200\). Mean: \(200 \div 5 = 40\) cm.
  2. Improvement: \((42 - 40) \div 40 \times 100 = 5\%\).

The answer: \((42 - 40) \div 40 \times 100 = 5\%\) better

Probability

Mammographer (breast screening radiographer)

Health and science

\(\displaystyle \dfrac{\text{cancer}}{\text{called back}} \times 100\)

If you're called back, how likely is it to be cancer?

NHS breast screening calls about 4 in every 100 people back for more tests. Of those 4, about 1 is diagnosed with breast cancer. Out of 1,000 people screened:

  1. Called back: \(1000 \times 4 \div 100 = 40\).
  2. Diagnosed with breast cancer: \(40 \div 4 = 10\).
  3. Chance a call-back is cancer: \(10 \div 40 \times 100 = 25\%\). So 3 in 4 people called back are fine.

The answer: \(10 \div 40 \times 100 = 25\%\) of call-backs are cancer

Football recruitment analyst

Health and scienceHigher

\(\displaystyle 1 - (1 - p_1)(1 - p_2)(1 - p_3)\)

p is each shot's chance of scoring

Why can't one attack be worth 1.67 goals?

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

Expected goals (xG) gives every shot a probability of being scored, from 0 to 1. Different models give slightly different values. One attack had three shots worth 0.41, 0.47 and 0.79 (example figures).

  1. xG for the attack: \(0.41 + 0.47 + 0.79 = 1.67\).
  2. You can't score 1.67 goals from one attack. The chance of no goal is \((1 - 0.41) \times (1 - 0.47) \times (1 - 0.79) = 0.0657\), so the chance of at least one goal is \(1 - 0.0657 = 0.9343\).

The answer: \(1 - 0.0657 = 0.9343\), the chance of at least one goal

Indices and exponential change

Nuclear medicine technologist

Health and scienceHigher

\(\displaystyle \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^n\)

n is the number of half-lives

How much tracer is left after a day?

The tracer used in many scans halves every 6 hours (its half-life). After 24 hours:

  1. Half-lives: \(24 \div 6 = 4\).
  2. Left: \((\tfrac{1}{2})^{4} = 1/16 = 0.0625\), so 6.25%.

The answer: \((\tfrac{1}{2})^{4} \times 100 = 6.25\%\) left after a day
